title: Ezekiel 32:1–16
context: Ezekiel 32:1–16 is dated to the twelfth year, twelfth month, first day, often placed in early 585 BC, after the fall of Jerusalem. The LORD tells the prophet to take up a lament over Pharaoh, who thought himself a young lion among the nations but is like a monster in the seas, churning and fouling the rivers. The LORD will catch him in a net, throw him on the land, and give him to the birds and animals; he will darken the heavens, the sun, and the moon over Egypt. Many peoples will be appalled at his fall, and kings will tremble. The sword of the king of Babylon will come, Egypt’s pride will be brought to nothing, and its waters will run clear. The unit ends by calling this a lament that the daughters of the nations will chant over Egypt. The images of the monster and darkened heavens echo 29:3–5 and prophetic pictures of the day of the LORD (compare Isaiah 13:10 and Joel 2:10). Both traditions read the lament as a sober announcement of judgment on pride, not as a celebration of suffering.

verses.text: In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, in the first day of the month, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet reports a word dated to the twelfth year, twelfth month, first day. Arminians see this oracle coming after Jerusalem’s fall, which gave Ezekiel’s warnings about Egypt added weight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the date as placing the lament after the city’s destruction. Both traditions hold the modern date loosely, often placing it in early 585 BC.

verses.text: “Son of man, take up a lamentation over Pharaoh king of Egypt, and tell him, ‘You were likened to a young lion of the nations; yet you are as a monster in the seas. You broke out with your rivers, and troubled the waters with your feet, and fouled their rivers.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet to lament over Pharaoh, who thought himself a young lion but is like a monster in the seas, fouling the rivers. Arminian readers see a lament that exposes Pharaoh’s self-image as false.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as recalling 29:3. Both traditions read the lament as a prophetic form announcing judgment, not as sympathy for Pharaoh’s cause.

verses.text: The Lord GOD says: “I will spread out my net on you with a company of many peoples. They will bring you up in my net.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says he will spread his net over Pharaoh with many peoples and haul him up. Arminians see God using nations as his net, bringing down the proud monster of the waters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over the nations. Both traditions note that similar net imagery appears in 12:13 and 17:20, and they read it poetically.

verses.text: I will leave you on the land. I will cast you out on the open field, and will cause all the birds of the sky to settle on you. I will satisfy the animals of the whole earth with you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will leave Pharaoh on the land and give him to the birds and animals. Arminian readers see the shame of an unburied death, which echoes 29:5.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reversal of Pharaoh’s greatness. Both traditions read the image soberly, as a picture of complete defeat.

verses.text: I will lay your flesh on the mountains, and fill the valleys with your height.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will lay Pharaoh’s flesh on the mountains and fill the valleys with his remains. Arminians see poetic exaggeration stressing the size of the fallen monster and the scope of the judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as poetic language. Both traditions treat the image soberly, without elaborating on its details.

verses.text: I will also water the land in which you swim with your blood, even to the mountains. The watercourses will be full of you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will water the land with Pharaoh’s blood to the mountains, filling the watercourses. Arminian readers see a picture recalling the plagues of Exodus, when the Nile turned to blood (Exodus 7:17–21).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the echo of the exodus as showing that the same God again judges Egypt. Both traditions read the verse soberly, as poetic description of judgment.

verses.text: When I extinguish you, I will cover the heavens and make its stars dark. I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon won’t give its light.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that when he extinguishes Pharaoh, he will darken the heavens, the stars, the sun, and the moon. Arminians see cosmic language describing the end of a great power, as if its fall shook the heavens.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and compare Isaiah 13:10 and Joel 2:10, where similar language is used of the day of the LORD. Both traditions read the language as poetic, and some note the echo of the darkness plague (Exodus 10:21–23).

verses.text: I will make all the bright lights of the sky dark over you, and set darkness on your land,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will darken all the lights of the sky over Pharaoh and set darkness on his land. Arminian readers see the completion of the cosmic picture, which stresses the seriousness of Egypt’s fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign rule over creation in judgment. Both traditions read the verse as continuing the poetic imagery of verse 7.

verses.text: “I will also trouble the hearts of many peoples, when I bring your destruction among the nations, into the countries which you have not known.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will trouble the hearts of many peoples when he brings Egypt’s destruction to unknown lands. Arminians see news of Egypt’s fall spreading widely and causing alarm among the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reach of God’s judgment. Both traditions note that some read the verse as referring to Egyptian captives taken to distant lands, and they hold that question open.

verses.text: Yes, I will make many peoples amazed at you, and their kings will be horribly afraid for you, when I brandish my sword before them. They will tremble at every moment, every man for his own life, in the day of your fall.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says many peoples will be appalled and their kings will tremble when he brandishes his sword in the day of Egypt’s fall. Arminian readers see the fear that spreads when nations see a great power humbled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s power displayed before the nations. Both traditions read the verse as showing that Egypt’s fall serves as a warning to other proud powers.

verses.text: For the Lord GOD says: “The sword of the king of Babylon will come on you.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says the sword of the king of Babylon will come on Egypt. Arminians see God naming the instrument of judgment once again, as in 30:10 and 30:24.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over Babylon’s campaigns. Both traditions note that how God uses Babylon is discussed at the Judges 9:23 box.

verses.text: I will cause your multitude to fall by the swords of the mighty. They are all the ruthless of the nations. They will bring the pride of Egypt to nothing, and all its multitude will be destroyed.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Egypt’s multitude will fall by the swords of ruthless nations, its pride will come to nothing, and its people be destroyed. Arminian readers see the humbling of pride as the central theme of the judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s justice against arrogance. Both traditions read the verse as summarizing the purpose of the Egypt oracles: to bring down Egypt’s pride.

verses.text: I will destroy also all its animals from beside many waters. The foot of man won’t trouble them any more, nor will the hoofs of animals trouble them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will destroy Egypt’s animals by its waters, so that no human foot or animal hoof will stir them. Arminians see the stillness of a land emptied by judgment, in contrast to the monster churning the waters in verse 2.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as completing the reversal of Pharaoh’s image. Both traditions read it as describing a land made desolate.

verses.text: Then I will make their waters clear, and cause their rivers to run like oil,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will make Egypt’s waters clear and its rivers run like oil. Arminian readers see the waters calmed after the monster is removed, a picture of stillness that follows judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as the reversal of verse 2. Both traditions note that some read the smooth waters as a sign of desolation, others as a sign of restored order, and they hold the image open.

verses.text: “When I make the land of Egypt desolate and waste, a land destitute of that of which it was full, when I strike all those who dwell therein, then they will know that I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that when he makes Egypt desolate and strikes its people, they will know he is the LORD. Arminians see the recognition formula once more, showing that judgment reveals God’s identity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s glory as the purpose of his judgments. Both traditions hold the formula as shared ground, which runs throughout the Egypt oracles.

verses.text: “ ‘ “This is the lamentation with which they will lament. The daughters of the nations will lament with this. They will lament with it over Egypt, and over all her multitude,” says the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says this is the lament that the daughters of the nations will chant over Egypt and its multitude. Arminian readers see the lament as a public mourning that will spread among the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the lament form as announcing judgment with sorrow. Both traditions read the closing as framing the whole unit as a dirge, not a song of triumph.
